title: Clear Creek County well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: In Clear Creek County, the median well depth is 252 ft and the median yield is 7 gpm. See what that means for drilling cost and reliability.
h1: Water wells in Clear Creek County, Colorado
intro_html:
Clear Creek County wells are classic mountain bedrock holes: variable depth, decent production for most homes, and some real outliers. The records show 3,454 wells with a reported total depth and 1,646 with a pump test, so we have a solid picture of how wells behave here in the rock between places like Idaho Springs, Georgetown, and St. Mary’s.

If you’re buying or building on a lot here, you want to understand how deep you’re likely to drill, what kind of gallons per minute are typical, and how much risk there is of hitting either a low producer or a very deep hole that runs up the bill.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Clear Creek County
sections.html:
The median well depth in Clear Creek County is 252 feet, with the middle half between 120 and 402 feet. That spread tells you bids have to account for a lot of uncertainty in fractured mountain bedrock.

About 19% of wells are under 100 feet, but 36% land between 100–300 feet and another 34% between 300–600 feet. Around 11% go past 600 feet, and the deepest recorded well hits 3,523 feet. That tiny group of very deep wells is what keeps drillers cautious on estimates.

Most wells are completed in unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers (5,344 wells) with a few tagged as Fractured Crystalline or Alluvial. In this kind of geology, two neighbors can have very different depths even on the same ridge.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water you can expect
sections.html:
Yield numbers here are better than many mountain counties. The median reported pump test is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 4.5 and 10.0 gpm. For a typical exempt household well, that’s plenty if you size storage correctly.

On the low side, only about 1% of tested wells report under 1 gpm, and 25% fall between 1–5 gpm. Most wells, 65%, produce between 5–15 gpm, and roughly 9% show 15+ gpm. That distribution is encouraging, but you still plan for the possibility of a marginal producer.

Household-use wells here are generally limited by Colorado’s 35 gpm pumping cap, so more yield than that doesn’t really change your day-to-day use, but low yield can drive decisions about storage tanks and water use habits.

sections.heading: Water levels and long-term trend in the mountains
sections.html:
Static water levels, where reported, are moderate for mountain country. The median depth to water is about 70 feet, with the middle half of readings between 30 and 120 feet below ground. That usually means a reasonable column of water standing in a typical 200–400 foot well.

By decade, median static levels were around 29 feet in the 1960s, 40 in the 1970s, then about 80 feet in the 1980s and 1990s. The 2010s show a median around 100 feet, with the 2020s back to about 80 feet. So water levels are deeper than they were in the 1960s but haven’t shown a steady, one-way decline.

This is all in fractured rock, so local fractures matter more than county-wide trends. Still, it’s smart to look at nearby well logs before committing to a build.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling here and when wells went in
sections.html:
Clear Creek County’s well history really ramps up in the 1970s and 1990s. The records show 47 permits from the 1950s and 153 in the 1960s, then a jump to 1,115 in the 1970s and 728 in the 1980s. The 1990s see another peak at 1,195 permits, followed by 798 in the 2000s.

More recently, there are 419 permits from the 2010s and 181 so far in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2025. That tells you there is still active building and replacement drilling going on across the county.

The most active drillers in the records are James Drilling Company (452 wells), Living Water Systems Inc. (325), and Walton (288). Most permits, about 87%, are for domestic or household use, with small shares for stock and monitoring wells.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Clear Creek County
sections.html:
Drilling here is through fractured granite and gneiss, so contractors typically charge by the foot. The model for this area shows a common range of about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s median depth of 252 feet, the drilled hole alone pencils out around $16,400–$25,200.

By the time you add casing, grouting, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished well at that median depth generally falls in the $22,400–$37,200 range. If your well ends up closer to the upper end of the 120–402 foot middle band, expect to be toward the high side of that.

Because 34% of wells run 300–600 feet and 11% exceed 600 feet, you should budget with some contingency instead of assuming you’ll hit an easy 150-foot hole.

sections.heading: Risks to watch: deep holes, mines, and water quality
sections.html:
The biggest financial risk here is depth. With 34% of wells in the 300–600 foot range and a notable 11% past 600 feet, a single extra 100 feet can add several thousand dollars to your cost. Low yield is less common but still a concern: about 1% of tested wells report under 1 gpm.

Clear Creek County has a lot of legacy mining and cleanup activity: records show about 3,790 historic mine features, 72 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 81 PFAS sampling or contamination locations within roughly 10 miles. That doesn’t mean your specific well is contaminated, but it does mean water testing is not optional.

Plan to coordinate well and septic locations so they meet setbacks and respect steep slopes, especially in areas like Idaho Springs, Empire, and the Georgetown–Silver Plume corridor.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a well lot in Clear Creek County
sections.html:
If you’re under contract on land here, start by pulling nearby well permits and logs. Look at depths relative to the 252-foot county median and see whether your ridge or gulch tends to be closer to 150 feet or 400+ feet. That helps you judge how much to pad your drilling budget.

For an existing well, ask for the permit number, construction report, and any yield or water-quality tests. With a county-wide median yield of 7.0 gpm and most wells between 4.5–10.0 gpm, many homes are fine, but you want to know if you’re in that lower 1–5 gpm band.

Because most aquifers are fractured bedrock, I’d also plan for a proper storage tank and pressure system, especially on higher, rocky sites above places like Floyd Hill or Echo Hills.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Clear Creek County, Colorado?
faq.a: In Clear Creek County, the median well depth is 252 feet, and the middle half of wells fall between 120 and 402 feet. About 19% are under 100 feet, 36% are 100–300 feet, 34% are 300–600 feet, and around 11% go deeper than 600 feet. The deepest well on record is 3,523 feet, so drillers here plan for a wide possible range.

faq.q: How many gallons per minute do Clear Creek County wells produce?
faq.a: From the wells that report pump tests, the median yield in Clear Creek County is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 4.5 and 10.0 gpm. Only about 1% of wells report under 1 gpm, 25% fall in the 1–5 gpm range, 65% are between 5–15 gpm, and roughly 9% are 15+ gpm. That’s usually adequate for a household well when paired with proper storage.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a water well in Clear Creek County?
faq.a: In fractured mountain bedrock here, typical drilling rates run about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s median depth of 252 feet, the drilled hole alone comes to roughly $16,400–$25,200. A complete well system with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical at that depth generally totals around $22,400–$37,200. Deeper wells in the 300–600 foot range will be higher, so budget a contingency.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Clear Creek County?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. The county has about 3,790 historic mine features, 72 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 81 PFAS sampling or contamination locations within roughly 10 miles, so there is potential for local impacts. Many private wells produce good water, but you should always do a full lab test for bacteria, metals, and other contaminants before relying on any well for drinking water.

faq.q: Are wells running dry in Clear Creek County, Colorado?
faq.a: Static water level data show medians around 29–40 feet below ground in the 1960s–70s, about 80 feet in the 1980s–90s, roughly 100 feet in the 2010s, and about 80 feet in the 2020s. That suggests water levels are deeper than in the 1960s but haven’t shown a simple, steady decline. In fractured bedrock, conditions vary a lot locally, so check nearby well logs and test any existing well for performance.
